facts.text: Taipei Botanical Garden, managed by the Taiwan Forestry Research Institute, has more than two thousand plant species on display.
The garden's areas include a Lotus Pond, a Bamboo Garden, a Succulent Plants Garden, a Fern Garden, a Buddhism Garden, and a Terminalia Catappa (Indian almond) plaza.
Lotus flowers bloom in the garden's Lotus Pond in summer; lotus seeds and the underground stem are well-known foods in Chinese cooking.
A lotus leaf stays clean because tiny bumps covered with wax let water drops roll off, and the rolling drops pick up dirt on the way.
Bamboo belongs to the grass family, and some kinds are among the fastest-growing plants in the world.
A new bamboo shoot usually reaches its full height within one growing season but needs several more seasons to become mature.
The garden's Buddhism Garden has the Bodhi tree, the kind of tree under which the Buddha is believed to have reached enlightenment.
Bodhi tree leaves are heart-shaped and end in a long drip tip, which helps water run off so the leaf dries quickly.
Ferns have no flowers or seeds; they reproduce with tiny spores, usually made in small clusters on the underside of the leaves and spread by wind.
The garden's plant collection includes cacti (family Cactaceae).
A cactus stores water in its thick stem, and its spines are leaves that changed shape; this cuts water loss and helps protect the plant from animals.
The large leaves of the Indian almond tree (Terminalia catappa) turn red before they drop, new leaves replace them quickly, and its wide, level branches give dense shade.
